beats.beat: Mr Rowe and the sexton find the main beam of the schoolroom cracked through with spring damp, and the repair will cost fifteen pounds against four in the poor box.
Rowe goes to the library above the draper's to post a subscription notice, where Miss Judith Vane is minding the counter for her brother.

Judith offers to keep the subscription book herself and suggests he ask certain parishioners by name rather than post a general notice; Rowe, harried, calls it parish politics dressed as advice, and she withdraws the offer at once.
Mrs Pike arrives with the news that Miss Louisa Marchmont, niece to the family holding the living, is to stay a fortnight at the gatehouse of the empty Amberlight House.
Mrs Pike declares this is the answer to everything and begins listing what Rowe must wear to be presented to her, ignoring his protest that he wants subscriptions, not a wife.

turn.note: Mrs Pike's closing line overrides Rowe's refusal and commits him to a courtship scheme he did not ask for, setting the next chapter's action in motion.

generic_prose.quote: There was a silence of the kind that a man afterwards spends a fortnight regretting.
generic_prose.replace_with: A concrete beat instead of a named feeling — Rowe fumbling his hat, or biting back a further word, would show the regret rather than announce it.

trope_note: Establishes enemies-of-manner friction cleanly through the sermon/counter exchange and introduces the meddling matchmaker at full throttle; the chaperone's-absence trope is correctly left for a later chapter.
fixes: Cut 'It barely stretches to coal.' — it restates the sentence before it and adds nothing the reader doesn't already have.
Trim 'She read it through before she answered, which took longer than he expected, and she read it twice.' to a single clause; the repetition of 'read' twice within one sentence is padding.
Cut or replace 'There was a silence of the kind that a man afterwards spends a fortnight regretting' with a physical action showing Rowe's discomfort rather than narrating the abstract feeling.
Tighten the poor-box paragraph — the Ludd family detail and the Easter illness can share one sentence instead of two to save words without losing the specific figures.
Consider trimming Mrs Pike's gatehouse speech; the maid and 'two-and-twenty' can be delivered in fewer clauses without losing the gossip texture.
